senses: A local chief or governor in parts of Malaysia and Indonesia.
examples: As soon as she graduated, Anwar Sadat dragged her and the classmate said to be responsible to a penghulu, who could officiate at the wedding.
Outdated provisions such as the appointment of forest rangers and penghulus to carry out duties, which are no longer relevant to modern Singapore, will also be removed.

senses: A person who engages in salvage work.
A raven or crow (typically Corvus corax).
ety: From Middle French corbeau, from Old French corb (from Latin corvus (“raven”)) or Old French corbel (“crow”) (from Late Latin corbellus, from Latin corvus). See also Norman corbin.
examples: And with them were some lang-gowned men who kenned the stars and would come out o' nights to talk to the deer and the corbies in their ain tongue.

senses: The ability to create or reproduce.
The ability to transcend personal interests to provide care and concern for younger and older generations.
ety: From generative + -ity. In the psychology sense coined by psychoanalyst Erik Erikson in 1950.
examples: Generativity is a broad property of systems that denotes the capacity of agents within them to connect to others and produce unanticipated outcomes and change.

senses: Either of two types of whitefish, Coregonus albula and Coregonus vandesius.
ety: Borrowed from Scots vendace, from Middle Scots *vendois, *vendis, from Middle French vendoise, vandoise (“dace”), from Old French vendoise, vandoise, from Late Latin *vindēsia, *vindisia, from Gaulish *windēsyā, from Proto-Celtic *windos (“white”). Compare modern French vandoise (“dace”).

senses: Synonym of wedding.
ety: From Hindi शादी (śādī) and Urdu شادی (śādī, “wedding; marriage”), from Persian شادی (šādī, “joy; rejoicing; wedding”), q.v.
examples: After my shaadi, I packed away those times. My duty was to my husband—and my three boys, also.

senses: Someone who owns or runs a tavern.
A bite or sting.
ety: Borrowed from Latin oestrus (“gadfly, sting, frenzy”), from Ancient Greek οἶστρος (oîstros), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eys-, used to form words denoting passion; see also Latin īra (“anger”), Lithuanian aistra (“violent passion”), Avestan 𐬀𐬈𐬯𐬨𐬀 (aesma, “anger”).

senses: Occurring after, or as a consequence of, sex.
examples: The patient suffered from postcoital malaise.

senses: The traditional garment of women in Ancient Rome, corresponding to the toga worn by men.
A chorister's surplice.
ety: Borrowed from Latin stola. Doublet of stole.

senses: The property or characteristic of being realizable.
A sea onion (Drimia maritima)
A mantis shrimp, Squilla mantis, from the Mediterranean
ety: From French scille, from Latin scilla. Doublet of scilla.

senses: A person who is skilled in or practices radiology.
A device, particularly one used in the printing of documents, which propels tiny droplets of ink to the paper.
An inkjet printer.
examples: The non-impact printers employ an electrostatic, thermal, inkjet or other non-impact mechanism to transfer the character image.
HP aims to improve energy efficiency of its inkjet and laserjet printers 40% by 2011 and to triple its use of recycled material in inkjet products by 2011.
Inkjets aren't as expensive as they used to be.

senses: Resembling a nightmare.
examples: Meanwhile, the everyday landscape becomes more nightmarish and unmanageable each year.
The dragon from under-earth, the nightmarish destroyer, lay destroyed as well, utterly without life.

People sometimes find the idea of buying and selling human bones nightmarish, but Ferry told The Washington Post he doesn’t think of it that way. He says he admires and respects the structure of bones.

senses: A Cossack headman or general.
Title used by the second-highest military commander in Poland and Lithuania (15th to 18th century).
ety: From Polish hetman, probably from Middle High German houbetman, heuptman (“commander”), from Old High German houbitman, from Proto-West Germanic *haubidamann. Compare modern German Hauptmann (“captain”), Haupt, Mann. The Polish e in hetman attests to a borrowing from an East Central German dialect, in which Middle High German -öu- gives -ē-. Doublet of head man.

senses: A broth or stock in Italian cookery.
A franchisor, a company which or person who grants franchises.
examples: But franchisers don't sell many of their thirty-three billion hamburgers per year in blue highway towns where chophouses must draw customers through continuing quality rather than national advertising.

senses: A facility that holds temporary art exhibitions, typically with loaned works.
examples: But in terms of contemporary art, the Hammer was operating more like a kunsthalle, a temporary home for a constantly changing roster of exhibitions.
Some—following the Kunsthalle model—do not have the collection on show and hold exhibitions of loaned works, but often mixed with works from the founder's collection.

senses: The National Higher Education Entrance Examination held annually in China as a prerequisite for entrance into most forms of higher education.
ety: From the Hanyu Pinyin romanization of Mandarin 高考 (gāokǎo, literally “higher [education] [entrance] examination”).

senses: Someone or something that disrupts.
An energy weapon in the form of a pistol.
A person who lives in the slums of cities.
ety: From slum + dog; first appeared in the 2008 British romantic comedy film Slumdog Millionaire.
examples: Priya, 17, has chosen to be a slumdog, and her life reads like a film script.
This trope appeals to audiences and award juries alike, while avoiding the obvious issue that there’s a lot of slumdogs who will never become millionaires.

senses: Redolent of dill (the herb).
The preservation of living organisms by employing low temperatures.
The tree Licania rigida, endemic to Brazil and Puerto Rico.
ety: Borrowed from Brazilian Portuguese oiticica, from Old Tupi.

senses: That can be towed.
A treaty or pact, in Spanish contexts.
A stylographic pen.
ety: Clipping of stylographic pen, from stylo- + graphic.
examples: Malone put his stylo in his pocket. There was no use reporting a lunatic.

senses: Synonym of superius.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin cantus (literally “song, chant”).

senses: Synonym of bioterrorism.
Having two parents.
A person who recycles, or a machine used to recycle.
Containing or releasing serotonin.
Involved in, or capable of modulating activity in, neurotransmission pathways that use serotonin receptor proteins.
The son of a shah.
ety: Borrowed from Classical Persian شاهزاده (šāhzāda), from شاه (šāh, “king”) + زاده (zāda, “offspring”).

senses: A visual art form from Maharashtra, India, involving singing and dancing.
Any traditional indigenous public ceremony.
ety: Borrowed from Marathi तमाशा (tamāśā), from Classical Persian تماشا (tamāšā), ultimately from Arabic مَشَى (mašā, “to walk”).

senses: A local political association
The fibre extracted from this plant known especially for its ability to hold shape, reduce wrinkling, and introduce a silky lustre used to make textiles, fishing nets, upholstery, etc.
The act of behaving like a dilettante, of being an amateur or dabbler, sometimes in the arts.
The act of enjoying the arts, being a connoisseur.
examples: The brawny craftsman finds it no child's play to mould his unpliant rugged masses; neither is guidance of men a dilettantism: what it becomes when treated as a dilettantism, we may see!
As Erasmus would find, the king and his advisers had a hard-edged attitude to scholarship that was worlds away from the enquiring dilettantism of Eltham.

senses: The act of towing.
A charge for towing.
Resembling a tooth, especially in shape
